rules.message: SQL embeds 2+ conditional-logic constructs (CASE WHEN branches / IF·IIF calls) — filtering/aggregation in SQL is fine, but conditional business rules here are hard to test and easy to duplicate. Consider whether the policy belongs in app code instead.

await on a store/ORM call (`Repository`/`Store`/`prisma`/`db`/`orm`/`tx`/`trx`) verified structurally inside a for/for-of/for-in/while/do-while statement or an array-iteration callback — checked against the parser's projected loop spans, not merely co-occurring with loop syntax somewhere in the same function — N+1 query pattern. HOUSE-CONVENTION PATH SCOPE, disclosed because nothing else announces it: this rule only ever scans `.ts` files under a `domains/<name>/routes/` or `api/` path SEGMENT, at ANY depth — `src/api/orders.ts` and `packages/svc/domains/billing/routes/list.ts` both count, and so do the same directories at the tree root. An awaited store call inside a loop ANYWHERE else in the tree (services, repositories, jobs, a differently-laid-out repo) is silently not checked, and zero findings from this rule means "not scanned there", never "no N+1 there". Batch the fetch (e.g. `findMany` with an `in` filter) instead of one call per item.

`store.count()`/`prisma.<model>.count()` called structurally inside a for/for-of/for-in/while/do-while statement or an array-iteration callback — checked against the parser's projected loop spans, not merely co-occurring with loop syntax somewhere in the same function — one count() per entity (N calls). Use a single GROUP BY query or a denormalized counter column.

A `.reduce(...)` call appears in the same function as a `findMany(`/raw `prepare(` call — a CO-OCCURRENCE heuristic on two independent patterns, NOT proof the reduce consumes that query's result: nothing links them, so a `.reduce(...)` over an unrelated array in a function that queries elsewhere fires just the same, and the finding anchors on the first `.reduce(...)`. The `fetch-many` arm is `\.findMany\s*\(|\bprepare\s*\(` — a bare `prepare(` call, with no `.all()` required. When they ARE connected: if the row set is large, a SQL aggregate (SUM/COUNT/GROUP BY) avoids transferring it; if small and reused, app-side is fine. Decide by data volume.

A `.filter(...)` call and a `.length` access both appear in the same function as a `findMany(`/raw `prepare(` call — a CO-OCCURRENCE heuristic on THREE independent patterns, NOT proof they form one `findMany().filter(...).length` chain: the three may match three unrelated lines, `.length` matches ANY `.length` access (a string's included), and the finding anchors on the first `.length`. The `fetch-many` arm is `\.findMany\s*\(|\bprepare\s*\(` — a bare `prepare(` call, with no `.all()` required. When they ARE connected: if the row set is large, a SQL aggregate (SUM/COUNT/GROUP BY) avoids transferring it; if small and reused, app-side is fine. Decide by data volume.

A `create`/`upsert`/`insert` write appears LEXICALLY AFTER an awaited `findOne`/`findById`/`findUnique` read in the NEAREST enclosing function — the reported line is the WRITE (the racing action), specifically the first one that actually follows a read. A trigger line that sits inside NO parser-projected function span (a class-property initializer, a top-level statement) is read as ungated, and the pairing there widens back to the whole scanned symbol span. The order is TEXTUAL, not dataflow: it does not prove the read feeds a branch that reaches the write, nor that the two touch the same row (a read of one table followed by an insert into another still fires). SAME-LINE NESTING RESIDUAL (a disclosed false negative shared by every rule that uses this order gate): on a single line "after" is decided by MATCH START OFFSET, so a read nested INSIDE the write call's own argument list reads as coming AFTER it and does not pair — an inline `await prisma.member.create({ data: { orgId: (await prisma.org.findUnique({ where: { slug } })).id } });` is silently NOT reported; only the multi-line spelling, or a same-line one whose read starts first, fires. HOUSE-CONVENTION PATH SCOPE, disclosed because nothing else announces it: this rule only ever scans `.ts`/`.tsx` files that sit under an `api/`, `routes/` or `controllers/` path segment or whose name ends in `handler.ts(x)`/`controller.ts(x)` (all three directory arms match at ANY depth, the tree ROOT included — the former anchoring asymmetry, under which a top-level `routes/` directory did not count, was judged and aligned to the `(?:^|/)` idiom, the same verdict `sql/nplus1`'s root anchor received) — the identical read-then-write race in a service, repository, use-case or job module is silently not scanned, and zero findings from this rule means "not scanned there", never "no TOCTOU there". SILENT VETO, equally undisclosed until now: the `absent` list kills the finding when ANY `try {` appears anywhere in the SAME scanned span — not a `try` shown to guard this write, just one in the same function. Since try/catch is near-universal in handler code, that veto is a large false-negative surface; it is deliberate (a caught unique-constraint violation is the common intentional spelling of check-then-act), but it means a handler wrapping unrelated work in try/catch reports nothing here. The other two vetoes are narrow by comparison: `FOR UPDATE`/`serializable`, and `ON CONFLICT`/`ON DUPLICATE KEY`. When it is the get-or-create/toggle shape it names, concurrent requests can both pass the check and both write (duplicate row / unique-constraint violation) — a TOCTOU race. Add a unique constraint and replace the check-then-act with an upsert; wrapping it in a `$transaction` alone does NOT close this race at the database's default READ COMMITTED isolation level — two concurrent transactions can both read empty and both insert. If you must keep the read+write shape, use `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` or serializable isolation instead.

A RAW-SQL write statement head (`INSERT INTO ...`, or `UPDATE <table> SET ...`) appears LEXICALLY AFTER a raw-SQL `SELECT` statement head in the NEAREST enclosing function — the reported line is the WRITE (the racing action), specifically the first one that actually follows a read. A trigger line that sits inside NO parser-projected function span (a class-property initializer, a top-level statement) is read as ungated, and the pairing there widens back to the whole scanned symbol span. This is the raw-SQL arm of the check-then-act family; the ORM arm is `sql/race-condition-toctou` (and `db/find-then-create-no-unique`), whose `findOne`/`findUnique` vocabulary and `api/`-`routes/`-`controllers/`-`*handler` path scope both structurally miss a raw-SQL backend, which is why this rule exists separately rather than as a widening of that one. WHAT IT DOES NOT PROVE: the order is TEXTUAL, not dataflow — it does not prove the read feeds a branch reaching the write, and it does NOT prove the two statements touch the SAME TABLE (a `SELECT` on one table followed by an `INSERT` into another still fires). Same-table matching would need the operation axis (SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE) on the `db-table` IO facts, which `parser-sql`'s `extract_statement_table_refs` does not return today, so this ships as an honest co-occurrence-plus-order heuristic, not as the precise version. UPPERCASE ONLY, and that is the precision gate, not an oversight: `"Select a date from the list"` is a syntactically valid `SELECT <col> FROM <table> <alias>`, so nothing but case separates raw SQL from English prose here — the same call `parser/parser-sql/src/consume.rs` makes for table extraction. The cost is a disclosed under-report: lowercase SQL is invisible to this rule. SAME-LINE NESTING RESIDUAL (shared by every rule using this order gate): on a single line "after" is decided by MATCH START OFFSET, so a read literal nested inside the write statement's own expression, but spelled after it, does not pair. NO `try` VETO, deliberately unlike `race-condition-toctou`: that sibling's `try` veto silences it in any handler that wraps anything at all in try/catch, and a caught unique-constraint violation is not the common spelling in raw-SQL backends. NO TRANSACTION VETO either, also deliberate: wrapping the read and the write in a transaction (or a D1 `batch`) does NOT close this race at the database's default READ COMMITTED isolation level, and the motivating shape is precisely a read that sits OUTSIDE the atomic write batch. The two vetoes that DO apply are the ones that actually serialize the check: a `FOR UPDATE`/`serializable` row lock, and an atomic conflict clause (`ON CONFLICT`/`ON DUPLICATE KEY`/`INSERT OR IGNORE`/`INSERT OR REPLACE`). Fix by making the check and the write one atomic statement — add a unique constraint plus `ON CONFLICT`, or make the write a conditional `UPDATE ... WHERE <version-column> = <value-read>` and check the affected-row count — or take a `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` row lock.

A CLOSED string literal contains `DELETE FROM <table>` with nothing else before the closing quote — the entire SQL statement is one complete literal with no interpolation, so there is provably no WHERE clause arriving from anywhere else, and this deletes every row in the table. Any sign the statement isn't fully closed right here — a `${...}` placeholder, a `'`/`"` string-concatenation `+`, or a trailing `?` bound-parameter tail — means we can't prove a WHERE is missing, so the rule stays silent rather than guess (never-guess). Migration paths are out of this rule's scope: a whole-table write in a committed migration is a deliberate one-time backfill, covered at disclosure severity by `sql/destructive-migration` instead — including Alembic's `alembic/versions/` layout, which is Python's dominant spelling of that directory and the only place in the whole dogfood corpus where this rule family matched a Python line at all. LANGUAGE SCOPE, stated because the matcher rides no host-language syntax at all: it is a quote character, the SQL keyword, the table name, and the same-line closing quote. Every language zzop parses spells a single-line SQL literal that way, so all of them are admitted (`.ts`/`.tsx`/`.js`/`.mjs`/`.cjs`, `.py`, `.java`, `.cs`, `.go`, `.rs`) — C#'s verbatim `@"..."` and Go's backtick raw string included, since the quote is still the character adjacent to `DELETE`. Two residuals ride along. (1) A MULTI-LINE statement is invisible: a Java text block, a Python triple-quoted string, a Go raw-string block or a multi-line C# `@"..."` puts `DELETE FROM` on a line carrying no quote, and a line-scan reads one line. (2) In `.py` the comment axis does not apply — zzop recognizes `//` as the comment/marker leader outside `.sql` and config files, so a `#`-commented-out DELETE is read as live code (measured 0 times across 16652 Python lines of the dogfood corpus) and `// zzop-delete-no-where-ok` is not writable Python. Add a WHERE clause, or if a full-table delete is genuinely intended, make it explicit (e.g. a dedicated `truncateTable()`/`deleteAll()` helper) and suppress with `// zzop-delete-no-where-ok` — in a `.py` file, where that comment cannot be written, narrow the rule through the `rules` config entry (a path `exclude` on it, or `off`) instead.

A CLOSED string literal contains `UPDATE <table> SET <assignments>` with nothing else before the closing quote — same discipline as `sql/delete-no-where`: no interpolation and no adjacent concatenation is visible anywhere in the statement, so no WHERE clause is arriving from anywhere this line-scan can see, and as written this updates every row in the table. Any sign the statement isn't fully closed right here — a `${...}` template placeholder, a Rust `format!` placeholder (`{}`, `{name}`, `{0}`) ANYWHERE between the `SET` and the closing quote, or a `'`/`"`/backtick string-concatenation `+` (including Rust's `"...".to_string() + expr` form) — means we can't tell whether a WHERE is missing, so the rule stays silent rather than guess (never-guess). What the hit does NOT prove, stated honestly rather than as the word `provably` this message used to carry: a line-scan reads ONE line, so a WHERE appended on a later line, or a `String::from("...") + expr` concatenation (whose `)` sits between the quote and the `+`, out of reach of the concat veto), would not be seen. Read a hit as "a complete whole-table UPDATE with no WHERE is visible on this line", and confirm the surrounding statement before acting. The Rust interpolating counterpart is `security/sql-format-interpolation` (warning): a `format!` that splices a value into an UPDATE lands there, not here — the placeholder exclusion above is what keeps the two from both firing on one line and telling the reader two different stories about it. The closing quote is matched BY KIND — only the same quote character that OPENED the literal terminates it, so a quote of a DIFFERENT kind inside the statement (`"UPDATE users SET name = 'anon'"`) is statement text, not a terminator. That is what makes the placeholder exclusion real rather than nominal: `format!("UPDATE users SET name = '{}'", name)` used to co-fire here at CRITICAL because the inner `'` was read as the closing quote, hiding the `{}` from the exclusion and breaking the partition this paragraph promises — that line is `security/sql-format-interpolation`'s alone. Migration paths are out of this rule's scope: a whole-table write in a committed migration is a deliberate one-time backfill, covered at disclosure severity by `sql/destructive-migration` instead — Alembic's `alembic/versions/` layout included, which is where the only real-corpus instances of this shape were measured. LANGUAGE SCOPE is the same set `sql/delete-no-where` states and for the same reason (the matcher rides no host-language syntax): `.ts`/`.tsx`/`.js`/`.mjs`/`.cjs`, `.py`, `.java`, `.cs`, `.go`, `.rs`. Three residuals come with it. (1) A MULTI-LINE statement is invisible — a Java text block, a Python triple-quoted string, a Go raw-string block or a multi-line C# `@"..."` puts the `UPDATE` on a line carrying no quote. (2) A printf-family `%s`/`%d` between the `SET` and the closing quote is read as a BOUND VALUE, exactly as `?` already is, NOT as evidence the statement is open — `cur.execute("UPDATE users SET active = %s", (0,))` is a genuine whole-table update and fires; the disclosed cost is that a `%s` splicing a whole CLAUSE (`"UPDATE t SET a = 1 %s" % cond`) is read the same way and would fire wrongly, which the `{`/`}` exclusion above does catch for `${...}` and `format!` because those spellings cannot mean a bound parameter. (3) In `.py` a `#`-commented-out UPDATE is read as live code and `// zzop-update-no-where-ok` is not writable Python — zzop recognizes `//` as the comment/marker leader outside `.sql` and config files. Add a WHERE clause, or if a full-table update is genuinely intended, make it explicit and suppress with `// zzop-update-no-where-ok` — in a `.py` file, where that comment cannot be written, narrow the rule through the `rules` config entry (a path `exclude` on it, or `off`) instead.

A syntax-anchored `TRUNCATE [TABLE] <table>` string literal appears in application code (not a migration) — the SQL analog of `redis/flushall-in-code`: TRUNCATE wipes every row in the table and, on most engines, cannot be rolled back once committed. LANGUAGE SCOPE is the set `sql/delete-no-where` states, for the same reason — the pattern is a quote character followed by the SQL keyword and nothing host-language-specific, so it holds in `.ts`/`.tsx`/`.js`/`.mjs`/`.cjs`, `.py`, `.java`, `.cs`, `.go` and `.rs` alike, C#'s verbatim `@"..."` and Go's backtick raw string included. The same two residuals apply: a MULTI-LINE statement (Java text block, Python triple-quoted string, Go raw-string block, multi-line C# `@"..."`) puts `TRUNCATE` on a line carrying no quote and is invisible to a line-scan; and in `.py` a `#`-commented-out TRUNCATE is read as live code, since zzop recognizes `//` as the comment/marker leader outside `.sql` and config files. Migration paths — `migrations/`, `migrate/`, and Alembic's `alembic/versions/` — are excluded here and covered at disclosure severity by `sql/destructive-migration`. Move destructive schema/data operations into a migration script outside the served codebase, or if this is a genuinely intentional runtime reset (e.g. a dedicated cache-reset job), suppress with `// zzop-truncate-in-app-code-ok` — in a `.py` file, where that comment cannot be written, narrow the rule through the `rules` config entry (a path `exclude` on it, or `off`) instead.

A destructive statement in a migration file: `DROP TABLE`/`DROP COLUMN`/`TRUNCATE [TABLE]`, or a closed-string-literal whole-table `DELETE FROM <table>` / `UPDATE <table> SET` with no WHERE (the same complete-literal shapes `sql/delete-no-where`/`sql/update-no-where` flag in app code — in a migration they are a deliberate one-time backfill, so they surface here at disclosure severity instead). An idempotent BOOTSTRAP preamble is excluded: a file that contains a `DROP TABLE IF EXISTS <x>;` followed by a `CREATE TABLE` with nothing between them but whitespace and `--` comments is a re-runnable schema bootstrap, which cannot destroy data, and every one of the seven measured findings of the earlier form was exactly that. ONE such adjacency anywhere in the file is enough, so the usual `0001_initial.sql` layout that lists every DROP first and every CREATE after is covered too (matched via its last DROP). `IF EXISTS` is required — a plain `DROP TABLE <x>` never qualifies, even directly above a `CREATE TABLE`. Residual limitation, stated honestly: line-scan tests one line at a time and the regex engine has no backreferences, so the DROP and the CREATE cannot be correlated BY TABLE NAME — the exclusion therefore silences the WHOLE file, meaning a genuinely destructive statement that shares a file with a bootstrap DROP-then-CREATE preamble is missed. Committed destructive migrations are usually deliberate, so this is info-level review-time disclosure, not a CI gate — its value is attention on NEW migrations at review, not archaeology of old ones. FILE SET, and the invariant that keeps this rule's handoff honest: the three critical siblings EXCLUDE migration paths, so whatever extension they admit in app code, this rule must admit under a migration directory — otherwise their message promises a disclosure nobody emits. It therefore accepts every extension they do (`.ts`/`.tsx`/`.js`/`.mjs`/`.cjs`, `.py`, `.java`, `.cs`, `.go`, `.rs`) plus `.sql`, under `migrations/`, `migration/`, `migrate/` and Alembic's `alembic/versions/`. That last spelling is Python's dominant one and was measured as the ONLY place in the whole dogfood corpus where a whole-table `UPDATE ... SET` literal appears in Python at all — five such lines, three of them surviving the WHERE veto; without this arm, admitting `.py` to the critical siblings would have reported those three deliberate backfills as CRITICAL. Verify the object name against the PR/ticket, back the data up first, and prefer a two-phase pattern (deprecate/stop-reading in one release, drop in a later one) over a same-release drop when the table might still be read. Suppress a vetted, reviewed migration with `// zzop-destructive-migration-ok` (or `-- zzop-destructive-migration-ok` in a `.sql` file); in a `.py` migration neither comment is writable Python — zzop recognizes `//` as the marker leader outside `.sql` and config files — so narrow that path through the `rules` config entry instead.

`SELECT * FROM` inside a string literal — over-fetching every column couples the caller to the table's exact shape (a later `ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN` silently changes what this query returns) and pulls columns nobody reads across the wire. LANGUAGE SCOPE is the set `sql/delete-no-where` states, for the same reason — an opening quote and then the SQL keywords, with no host-language syntax in the pattern — so `.ts`/`.tsx`/`.js`/`.mjs`/`.cjs`, `.py`, `.java`, `.cs`, `.go` and `.rs` are all admitted, C#'s verbatim `@"..."` and Go's backtick raw string included. The MULTI-LINE residual is larger here than for the destructive siblings, because a long SELECT is exactly the statement people break across lines: a Java text block, a Python triple-quoted string, a Go raw-string block or a multi-line C# `@"..."` whose `SELECT *` sits on its own line carries no quote there, and a line-scan cannot see it. In `.py`, a `#`-commented-out query is read as live code (zzop recognizes `//` as the comment/marker leader outside `.sql` and config files). CO-FIRING with `security/sql-string-concat` is intended, not a duplicate: on a Java line like `"SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '" + name + "'"` that rule reports the INJECTION shape and this one reports the OVER-FETCH, two independent defects with two different repairs (bind the parameter; name the columns) — the same ruling `security/weak-crypto` and `security/weak-password-hash` carry on one credential line. Neither rule's silence would imply the other's. List the columns you actually use instead.

A `LIKE` pattern with a leading `%` wildcard (e.g. `LIKE '%term'`) can't use a standard B-tree index prefix — the engine falls back to a full table/index scan on every call. LANGUAGE SCOPE is the widest of this pack, because the anchor is entirely INSIDE the SQL: `LIKE` followed by a SQL string quote and a `%`, with not one character of host-language syntax in it. Admitted in `.ts`/`.tsx`/`.js`/`.mjs`/`.cjs`, `.py`, `.java`, `.cs`, `.go` and `.rs`. That very portability is what makes one exclusion necessary, and it is the only language-shaped thing here: in the printf family a `%` immediately followed by a conversion letter and then the closing quote is a PLACEHOLDER, not a wildcard — `fmt.Sprintf("... LIKE '%s'", term)` in Go, `String.format` in Java, `"... LIKE '%s'" % term` and the named `'%(term)s'` form in Python all substitute the whole pattern at runtime, so claiming a leading wildcard there would be a claim about text this rule never sees. Those lines are excluded. The exclusion is deliberately narrow — it requires the quote to close IMMEDIATELY after the conversion letter, so `LIKE '%sale%'` (a real leading wildcard that happens to start `%s`) still fires, and `LIKE '%' + @term` / `LIKE '%%%s%%'` still fire because the `%` there is genuinely a wildcard. Its disclosed cost is the one-character search `LIKE '%s'` meaning "ends with s", which is now silent. Python's bare `LIKE %s` (psycopg's unquoted bound parameter) never matched in the first place: the pattern requires a quote between `LIKE` and the `%`. In `.py` a `#`-commented-out query is read as live code, since zzop recognizes `//` as the comment/marker leader outside `.sql` and config files. If this needs to stay a substring/suffix search, reach for full-text search or a reversed-column index; a trailing-only wildcard (`LIKE 'term%'`) stays index-friendly. Suppress a vetted case (small table, offline query) with `// zzop-like-leading-wildcard-ok` — in a `.py` file, where that comment cannot be written, narrow the rule through the `rules` config entry (a path `exclude` on it, or `off`) instead.
